title: Steel shot and chokes
summary: Steel shot is hard and does not squeeze in the choke, so it patterns tighter. Which chokes suit it, how to read the proof marks, and what this means at Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting grounds that require steel.

body.html: Some grounds, especially near water or in protected areas, allow only lead-free shot, most often steel or soft iron. The shot itself is covered in Lead, steel and soft iron. Here we look at what it means for chokes.

A lead pellet is soft and deforms slightly as it passes through the choke. A steel pellet is hard and does not squeeze. So the same choke gives a noticeably tighter pattern with steel, and many shooters fit a choke one step more open: 1/4 instead of 1/2.

Hard steel also puts more stress on the choke. Many makers and distributors advise chokes no tighter than modified (1/2) with standard steel loads. For high performance steel (the more powerful kind, explained below) some suggest 1/4 at most. A full choke with steel is mostly not advised. The exact limit depends on the gun, so read the maker's manual.
Chokes made for steel are often marked 'Steel' or 'Steel OK', and some carry 'Lead only'. If a choke has no marking and you have no manual, ask a gunsmith.

html: Old thin-walled barrels, especially with a fixed full choke, can be damaged by steel: a ring bulge may appear near the muzzle.
Steel cartridges come in two classes under the C.I.P. rules (the common test standards for guns and cartridges used in most of Europe): standard steel and high performance steel.
Standard steel may be fired in a gun in good condition with the usual proof marks. These are the stamps a testing station (proof house) puts on a gun after test-firing it.
High performance steel may be fired only in a gun that has passed a separate steel-shot test; its barrels carry a lily-shaped stamp (fleur-de-lis), often with the words 'Steel Shot'.
Steel clay loads are usually standard steel. Check the box and your gun's papers; if in doubt, ask a gunsmith.

body.html: Going to a ground that requires steel? Find out in advance which cartridges are allowed and bring chokes made for steel. Before a competition, shoot those cartridges in practice to see how your pattern changes.

key_points.html: Steel shot does not squeeze in the choke and patterns tighter.
With steel, many shooters go one choke more open.
Many makers advise no tighter than 1/2 with steel; full is mostly not advised.
Look for a 'Steel' marking on the choke and read the manual.
Old thin-walled barrels can be damaged; high performance steel needs the fleur-de-lis proof.

did_you_know.html: A steel pellet is about 30% lighter than a lead pellet of the same size, so it loses speed sooner. That is why steel users often choose slightly larger shot, where the ground's rules allow it.

quiz.q: Why does steel shot pattern tighter than lead through the same choke?

options.text: Steel is heavier than lead shot
Hard steel pellets do not squeeze in the choke
Steel cartridges hold many more pellets
Steel shot leaves the barrel faster

quiz.explain: Soft lead deforms slightly in the choke; hard steel does not, so it stays more compact.

quiz.q: Which choke is mostly not advised with steel shot?
quiz.explain: Full choke with steel is mostly not advised; the exact limit is in the maker's manual.

quiz.q: How do you find out whether a choke suits steel?
